[](https://substack.com/redirect/6666307e-b39b-4087-8223-e7c77afed167?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Two of Idaho's ag men recently sat down on [a podcast](https://substack.com/redirect/26eb13a0-76ae-44b8-a54f-611e0ccd8e53?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and laid out the whole case for keeping cheap slave labor flowing into this state. Worth listening to. Worth answering, too.
So here's every argument in the Cheap Slave Labor CatechismTM, and what's wrong with each one.
## "A federal problem that needs to be fixed federally, and it needs to pay attention to our industries."
There it is, in one sentence.
Notice the order of the clauses. First, the nation has a problem. Second, the fix has to be tailored to the convenience of the men who profited from the problem.
For 40 years the American worker has been told the border needs a "comprehensive solution," and every comprehensive solution shows up with the same two halves: amnesty now, enforcement later. Reagan tried that in 1986. Three million people who broke the law to get here were legalized, employer sanctions went into the law, and then the sanctions sat there for four decades doing nothing, because they were never meant to do anything, and we're still paying the bill and so are our kids.
Anyone offering to run it again is either a fool or is counting on you being one.
## "That's what Trump did. Shut the gate. That's all we had to do."
Great. So why is the very next paragraph a request to prop it open for one privileged category of employer?
That's a service entrance with a key that goes to whoever keeps a lobbyist in Washington.
And a border enforced by executive discretion expires with the administration that ordered it, which the men who want permanent access to cheap slave labor understand better than anybody. They're happy to let the gate close for the evening news and then go negotiate their own door around back.
## "Find me a first world country where you're not going to find immigrants doing some of these jobs."
Ooh, my turn...
_Find me a first world country where the median man can buy a house on one income the way his grandfather did._
That comparison cuts harder the other way and everyone knows it.
The premise is wrong anyway. For decades (before 1965) this country ran the tightest immigration regime in its modern history, and that stretch produced the largest expansion of the American middle class ever recorded. A tight labor market is the only reliable friend the working man has ever had. And every person who tells you otherwise is buying labor rather than selling it.
## "Our kids don't want to do those jobs, because they have better opportunities."
Americans won't do the job at those wages, in those conditions, next to people who were brought in specifically to hold both down. Say the whole sentence out loud and the argument falls apart.
_**There 's no such thing as a job Americans won't do.**_
But there are definitely wages and conditions Americans won't accept, and keeping both exactly where they are is the entire point of importing the labor.
Ask what happened when Congress killed the Bracero program in 1964. The growers swore the tomatoes would rot in the fields. Instead the harvest got mechanized and California grew more tomatoes than before. Scarcity of labor is the mother of invention. And cheap slave labor in unlimited supply is the mother of doing it in 2026, which is exactly what the industries that have imported wage slaves for 60 years are still doing.
And follow their own logic out a few years. If cheap foreign labor is the entry ramp to a better life, and our own kids have already climbed off it, then we need another wave in 20 years. And another after that. Forever. It's a supply chain with a constant drip of foreign wage slaves, and a country that has to import a permanent underclass every generation to protect its margins is eating itself.
## "Calling it slave labor? Are you kidding me. They're well taken care of."
The objection was never that any individual employer is cruel. The objection is that labor tied to one employer by visa status can't bargain and can't quit without leaving the country, so it can't do the one thing free labor does by its nature, which is push wages up.
That's the whole point of the arrangement. It's not a bug, it's a feature.
And that's just the legal half. Dairy doesn't even get the legal half, because H-2A covers seasonal work and cows get milked in February, so the dairies are locked out of the program entirely.
But they'll say the quiet part in our own Capitol if you sit through enough testimony. Bob Naerebout of the Idaho Dairymen's Association told legislators that as much as 70% of the industry's workforce might be here illegally. The IDA's own commissioned report puts dairy at 90% foreign born with roughly half being illegal. Their economist warned that enforcing the law would cut dairy output 45%. Nobody's denying that. They're describing a dependency they built on purpose, on the record, and then asking us to protect it.
Ask anyone who works the borders ([I did a few months back when I spent time with law enforcement in Arizona](https://substack.com/redirect/1504d13a-2c53-48d1-aa25-2b784e23255b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)) and they'll tell you that nobody crosses without the cartels allowing it and taking their cut. _Not a single person._
So the foreign workforce that shows up here is already owned by somebody, with a debt attached, no papers, and no standing to complain to anyone about anything. Call that a labor market if you like. I call it a trafficking pipeline with a milking parlor at the end of it.
So when a man tells you those workers are "well taken care of," understand you're hearing an old southern slavery argument. George Fitzhugh, the Virginia lawyer who wrote the most thorough defense of slavery this country ever produced, made the same case in 1857:
_" The slave is taken care of, whether employed or not."_
He wasn't lying, either.
He was describing a real feature of the system and offering it as the reason you shouldn't look too hard at the rest of it. That's what "well taken care of" has always been for.
## "The far right wants to hunt them all down, and that's not Trump's position."
Correct. That's the problem.
The gate got shut, and the part that actually mattered never showed up. Nobody indicted a dairy executive. There was no serious I-9 audit program. E-Verify still isn't mandatory, and the ag and LEO lobby kills it in Boise every single time it's introduced. And 287(g) still isn't mandatory either.
You could end this in 18 months without one dramatic raid by making it a felony to profit from illegal labor, then convict somebody prominent enough that the rest of the industry reads the news and does the math.
People who broke the law to get here should go home.
_All of them_.
There's no version of a country with borders where the penalty for crossing one illegally is a work permit, a benefits package, and free stuff. Removal is the ordinary operation of immigration law, and calling it an atrocity is how you get 20 more years of nothing.
But the man who hired them should be in worse trouble than the trafficked person he hired. He's the citizen. He took the oath, he knew the law, and he broke it in his own country for profit. Here's a video of Charlie Kirk unpacking this exact sentiment at a conference of roofers who admit that they hire illegals to prop up their industry:

The problem is that every enforcement regime since 1986 has pointed at the workers and left the employers alone. There are dairies in Idaho running the same arrangement they were running 30 years ago, and it lasts because the ag lobby pays for legislators who protect it. The lobby writes the talking points. Their legislators repeat them in committee and the enforcement bills die, often without a recorded vote. Cheap labor stays cheap. Everybody at that table knows the deal, and none of them ever have to say a word about it in public.
The Farm Bureau guy is right that Trump isn't saying what the base is saying.
Trump didn't go far enough, and the half he skipped is the half that would've worked. The base is the people who lost the plant and watched main street hollow out and voted for the one man who'd say build the wall without apologizing. They voted to get the country back, and a photo op at the Rio Grande with a carve-out for agriculture is, and I want to be precise here, not that.
America First means America First. It doesn't come with an exemption for whoever keeps the best lobbyist in Boise or DC.
## "Go back to Mitt Romney. That's your adult in the room."
Mitt Romney ran on self-deportation in 2012 and had abandoned it by 2013, when he joined the chorus for the Gang of Eight bill. He's the mascot of the Conservative Inc. Republicanism that lost the country: fight to the death over the marginal tax rate, surrender without a shot on the border, the trade deficit, and the wars.
If he's your standard for a statesman, the word doesn't mean anything anymore.
## "A state legislator making noise about immigration is looking out for their publicity, not your interests."
Here's the thing about the man who says that. The Farm Bureau guy on the podcast was publicly thanked, by name, alongside the lobbyist for the Dairymen's Association, for his work on the Securing Agriculture's Workforce Act. The President of the Farm Bureau even went on record backing it too. So the CEO telling Idaho legislators to stay in our lane has been working a federal legalization bill for the workforce his members employ.
He's not against politicians getting involved in immigration.
He's against the ones he can't control (or, buy).
And it's funny coming from a man sitting in a studio with a multi-millionaire commercial developer, recording an episode of the developer's podcast, in the middle of a three-week guest-hosting run the developer announced in the intro, while the two of them wax eloquent about the new headquarters going up next to the Capitol, sited there because, as he puts it, "Boise is where the laws happen."
Then they get to immigration, and the problem is that state legislators are seeking attention?
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/53306573-0d4f-4e21-8395-852c316d7c33?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
It isn't even an original line.
The dairyman lobbyist says the same thing, word for word: _" This is a federal issue, not a state issue." _Same script, same legislators repeating it, same bills dying.
The claim underneath is that Idaho has no legitimate voice on the one question that most reshapes our schools, our hospitals, our towns, our families, and what a working man in this state gets paid, because it's a federal matter and we should leave it to the professionals. Yes, the same professionals who've refused to act for four decades. And the same ones his own federation lobbies to keep refusing.
So Idahoans get no representative anywhere. Convenient.
But 287(g) is a federal statute written so state and local agencies can act, and more than 1,400 of those agreements are live across 40 states, including the Idaho patriots who didn't wait for permission: sheriffs in Kootenai, Franklin, Caribou, Washington, Bonneville, Bingham, and Owyhee counties, plus the city of Post Falls, whose police department signed on in June with Mayor Randy Westlund and Chief Mark Brantl backing it publicly.
Florida required its counties to sign, all 67 complied, and Florida now runs the most saturated enforcement footprint in the country. Georgia and Texas did this too.
So the idea that an Idaho legislator has no business having an opinion about this is laughable, and the people making that argument know it's laughable. It's a request that we sit down and be quiet.
I sat through hours of testimony on the immigration bills we brought a few months ago, so let me tell you how this actually works.
Everybody shows up. The Idaho Sheriffs' Association came out hard against our 287(g) bill, put it in writing, an open letter to the whole Legislature saying they were unequivocally opposed. The police chiefs lined up the same way. Their reasons were the ones you'd expect: it costs money, it pulls deputies off patrol, they weren't consulted, they don't want to be bound to whatever the feds decide five years from now. Fine. That's how it's supposed to go, and I'll argue with them (and I did) openly any time.
And The Idaho Dairymen's Association shows up too. They've been testifying against these bills for years, not just this last session. E-Verify comes up, they're there. Anything that touches their members' workforce, they're there. In February they held a press conference in the Capitol to roll out a report they paid for, warning that enforcement would cost the state $5.1 billion.
So this isn't a smoke-filled room.
That's the part people get wrong when they imagine how the sausage gets made.
Here's what actually happens. A man walks into an Idaho committee room and tells elected officials, out loud, on the record, that a large share of his industry's workforce is here illegally. His own commissioned report says half the dairy workforce is unauthorized. Their own guy told legislators years ago it might be 70%. And then, having said that, he asks us not to pass a bill that would check.
And we don't. That's the part you need to sit with. Not that anybody lied... _but that nobody had to._ The admission and the request go in the same breath, into a microphone, in a building full of Republicans who ran on the border, and the bill dies anyway. Sometimes without a recorded vote, so there's nobody's name to look up afterward.
That's the game. It isn't hidden. It's just never punished.
## "The right raises money off it, the left raises money off it."
Half true, and the false half is the important one. The two parties aren't opposites here. They fight about the paperwork and agree completely about the flow, because the donor class of both of them wants the flow.
The Chamber of Commerce and the immigration lawyers are two hands on the same body, and the fundraising theater exists to hide how much they agree.
The people aren't divided on this one.
Washington is united against them.
## "$20 milk. Lettuce from Mexico."
The price on the carton is the smallest part of the price.
Add the schooling. Add the emergency rooms. Add the housing pressure in every Idaho town within driving distance of a big dairy. _And add the wages held down across every trade that has to compete with subsidized labor._

Idahoans pay all of it, while the savings go on one set of books and the costs go on everybody else's.
Then the argument eats itself.
Farm Bureau guy says he wants the food grown here, by people paid decently, so we aren't at the mercy of Mexico for lettuce. Good. That's economic nationalism and he's right. But he wants it grown here using the same cheap foreign labor he'd be buying if the farm were in Mexico, so the deal hasn't changed at all, he's just moved the border so the cheap part happens on our side of it, with our schools and our hospitals absorbing the difference.
You can't wave the flag to keep the farm and then dissolve the country's labor market to keep the margin.
It's a passive-aggressive threat: _vote our way or your groceries get expensive._
A country is a people before it's an economy. But once the people are an input cost, there's nothing left worth defending.

clean_body: Two of Idaho's ag men recently sat down on a podcast and laid out the whole case for keeping cheap slave labor flowing into this state. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more | | | Sep 3 | | | | | | | | | | | | Two of Idaho's ag men recently sat down on and laid out the whole case for keeping cheap slave labor flowing into this state. Worth listening to. Worth answering, too. So here's every argument in the Cheap Slave Labor CatechismTM, and what's wrong with each one. "A federal problem that needs to be fixed federally, and it needs to pay attention to our industries." There it is, in one sentence. Notice the order of the clauses. First, the nation has a problem. Second, the fix has to be tailored to the convenience of the men who profited from the problem. For 40 years the American worker has been told the border needs a "comprehensive solution," and every comprehensive solution shows up with the same two halves: amnesty now, enforcement later. Reagan tried that in 1986. Three million people who broke the law to get here were legalized, employer sanctions went into the law, and then the sanctions sat there for four decades doing nothing, because they were never meant to do anything, and we're still paying the bill and so are our kids. Anyone offering to run it again is either a fool or is counting on you being one. "That's what Trump did. Shut the gate. That's all we had to do." Great. So why is the very next paragraph a request to prop it open for one privileged category of employer? That's a service entrance with a key that goes to whoever keeps a lobbyist in Washington. And a border enforced by executive discretion expires with the administration that ordered it, which the men who want permanent access to cheap slave labor understand better than anybody. They're happy to let the gate close for the evening news and then go negotiate their own door around back. "Find me a first world country where you're not going to find immigrants doing some of these jobs." Ooh, my turn... Find me a first world country where the median man can buy a house on one income the way his grandfather did. That comparison cuts harder the other way and everyone knows it. The premise is wrong anyway. For decades (before 1965) this country ran the tightest immigration regime in its modern history, and that stretch produced the largest expansion of the American middle class ever recorded. A tight labor market is the only reliable friend the working man has ever had. And every person who tells you otherwise is buying labor rather than selling it. "Our kids don't want to do those jobs, because they have better opportunities." Americans won't do the job at those wages, in those conditions, next to people who were brought in specifically to hold both down. Say the whole sentence out loud and the argument falls apart. There 's no such thing as a job Americans won't do. But there are definitely wages and conditions Americans won't accept, and keeping both exactly where they are is the entire point of importing the labor. Ask what happened when Congress killed the Bracero program in 1964. The growers swore the tomatoes would rot in the fields. Instead the harvest got mechanized and California grew more tomatoes than before. Scarcity of labor is the mother of invention. And cheap slave labor in unlimited supply is the mother of doing it in 2026, which is exactly what the industries that have imported wage slaves for 60 years are still doing. And follow their own logic out a few years. If cheap foreign labor is the entry ramp to a better life, and our own kids have already climbed off it, then we need another wave in 20 years. And another after that. Forever. It's a supply chain with a constant drip of foreign wage slaves, and a country that has to import a permanent underclass every generation to protect its margins is eating itself. "Calling it slave labor? Are you kidding me. They're well taken care of." The objection was never that any individual employer is cruel. The objection is that labor tied to one employer by visa status can't bargain and can't quit without leaving the country, so it can't do the one thing free labor does by its nature, which is push wages up. That's the whole point of the arrangement. It's not a bug, it's a feature. And that's just the legal half. Dairy doesn't even get the legal half, because H-2A covers seasonal work and cows get milked in February, so the dairies are locked out of the program entirely. But they'll say the quiet part in our own Capitol if you sit through enough testimony. Bob Naerebout of the Idaho Dairymen's Association told legislators that as much as 70% of the industry's workforce might be here illegally. The IDA's own commissioned report puts dairy at 90% foreign born with roughly half being illegal. Their economist warned that enforcing the law would cut dairy output 45%. Nobody's denying that. They're describing a dependency they built on purpose, on the record, and then asking us to protect it. Ask anyone who works the borders () and they'll tell you that nobody crosses without the cartels allowing it and taking their cut. Not a single person. So the foreign workforce that shows up here is already owned by somebody, with a debt attached, no papers, and no standing to complain to anyone about anything. Call that a labor market if you like. I call it a trafficking pipeline with a milking parlor at the end of it. So when a man tells you those workers are "well taken care of," understand you're hearing an old southern slavery argument. George Fitzhugh, the Virginia lawyer who wrote the most thorough defense of slavery this country ever produced, made the same case in 1857: " The slave is taken care of, whether employed or not." He wasn't lying, either. He was describing a real feature of the system and offering it as the reason you shouldn't look too hard at the rest of it. That's what "well taken care of" has always been for. "The far right wants to hunt them all down, and that's not Trump's position." Correct. That's the problem. The gate got shut, and the part that actually mattered never showed up. Nobody indicted a dairy executive. There was no serious I-9 audit program. E-Verify still isn't mandatory, and the ag and LEO lobby kills it in Boise every single time it's introduced. And 287(g) still isn't mandatory either. You could end this in 18 months without one dramatic raid by making it a felony to profit from illegal labor, then convict somebody prominent enough that the rest of the industry reads the news and does the math. People who broke the law to get here should go home. All of them. There's no version of a country with borders where the penalty for crossing one illegally is a work permit, a benefits package, and free stuff. Removal is the ordinary operation of immigration law, and calling it an atrocity is how you get 20 more years of nothing. But the man who hired them should be in worse trouble than the trafficked person he hired. He's the citizen. He took the oath, he knew the law, and he broke it in his own country for profit. Here's a video of Charlie Kirk unpacking this exact sentiment at a conference of roofers who admit that they hire illegals to prop up their industry: The problem is that every enforcement regime since 1986 has pointed at the workers and left the employers alone. There are dairies in Idaho running the same arrangement they were running 30 years ago, and it lasts because the ag lobby pays for legislators who protect it. The lobby writes the talking points. Their legislators repeat them in committee and the enforcement bills die, often without a recorded vote. Cheap labor stays cheap. Everybody at that table knows the deal, and none of them ever have to say a word about it in public. The Farm Bureau guy is right that Trump isn't saying what the base is saying. Trump didn't go far enough, and the half he skipped is the half that would've worked. The base is the people who lost the plant and watched main street hollow out and voted for the one man who'd say build the wall without apologizing. They voted to get the country back, and a photo op at the Rio Grande with a carve-out for agriculture is, and I want to be precise here, not that. America First means America First. It doesn't come with an exemption for whoever keeps the best lobbyist in Boise or DC. "Go back to Mitt Romney. That's your adult in the room." Mitt Romney ran on self-deportation in 2012 and had abandoned it by 2013, when he joined the chorus for the Gang of Eight bill. He's the mascot of the Conservative Inc. Republicanism that lost the country: fight to the death over the marginal tax rate, surrender without a shot on the border, the trade deficit, and the wars. If he's your standard for a statesman, the word doesn't mean anything anymore. "A state legislator making noise about immigration is looking out for their publicity, not your interests." Here's the thing about the man who says that. The Farm Bureau guy on the podcast was publicly thanked, by name, alongside the lobbyist for the Dairymen's Association, for his work on the Securing Agriculture's Workforce Act. The President of the Farm Bureau even went on record backing it too. So the CEO telling Idaho legislators to stay in our lane has been working a federal legalization bill for the workforce his members employ. He's not against politicians getting involved in immigration. He's against the ones he can't control (or, buy). And it's funny coming from a man sitting in a studio with a multi-millionaire commercial developer, recording an episode of the developer's podcast, in the middle of a three-week guest-hosting run the developer announced in the intro, while the two of them wax eloquent about the new headquarters going up next to the Capitol, sited there because, as he puts it, "Boise is where the laws happen." Then they get to immigration, and the problem is that state legislators are seeking attention? | | ---|---|--- It isn't even an original line. The dairyman lobbyist says the same thing, word for word: " This is a federal issue, not a state issue." Same script, same legislators repeating it, same bills dying. The claim underneath is that Idaho has no legitimate voice on the one question that most reshapes our schools, our hospitals, our towns, our families, and what a working man in this state gets paid, because it's a federal matter and we should leave it to the professionals. Yes, the same professionals who've refused to act for four decades. And the same ones his own federation lobbies to keep refusing. So Idahoans get no representative anywhere. Convenient. But 287(g) is a federal statute written so state and local agencies can act, and more than 1,400 of those agreements are live across 40 states, including the Idaho patriots who didn't wait for permission: sheriffs in Kootenai, Franklin, Caribou, Washington, Bonneville, Bingham, and Owyhee counties, plus the city of Post Falls, whose police department signed on in June with Mayor Randy Westlund and Chief Mark Brantl backing it publicly. Florida required its counties to sign, all 67 complied, and Florida now runs the most saturated enforcement footprint in the country. Georgia and Texas did this too. So the idea that an Idaho legislator has no business having an opinion about this is laughable, and the people making that argument know it's laughable. It's a request that we sit down and be quiet. I sat through hours of testimony on the immigration bills we brought a few months ago, so let me tell you how this actually works. Everybody shows up. The Idaho Sheriffs' Association came out hard against our 287(g) bill, put it in writing, an open letter to the whole Legislature saying they were unequivocally opposed. The police chiefs lined up the same way. Their reasons were the ones you'd expect: it costs money, it pulls deputies off patrol, they weren't consulted, they don't want to be bound to whatever the feds decide five years from now. Fine. That's how it's supposed to go, and I'll argue with them (and I did) openly any time. And The Idaho Dairymen's Association shows up too. They've been testifying against these bills for years, not just this last session. E-Verify comes up, they're there. Anything that touches their members' workforce, they're there. In February they held a press conference in the Capitol to roll out a report they paid for, warning that enforcement would cost the state $5.1 billion. So this isn't a smoke-filled room. That's the part people get wrong when they imagine how the sausage gets made. Here's what actually happens. A man walks into an Idaho committee room and tells elected officials, out loud, on the record, that a large share of his industry's workforce is here illegally. His own commissioned report says half the dairy workforce is unauthorized. Their own guy told legislators years ago it might be 70%. And then, having said that, he asks us not to pass a bill that would check. And we don't. That's the part you need to sit with. Not that anybody lied... but that nobody had to. The admission and the request go in the same breath, into a microphone, in a building full of Republicans who ran on the border, and the bill dies anyway. Sometimes without a recorded vote, so there's nobody's name to look up afterward. That's the game. It isn't hidden. It's just never punished. "The right raises money off it, the left raises money off it." Half true, and the false half is the important one. The two parties aren't opposites here. They fight about the paperwork and agree completely about the flow, because the donor class of both of them wants the flow. The Chamber of Commerce and the immigration lawyers are two hands on the same body, and the fundraising theater exists to hide how much they agree. The people aren't divided on this one. Washington is united against them. "$20 milk. Lettuce from Mexico." The price on the carton is the smallest part of the price. Add the schooling. Add the emergency rooms. Add the housing pressure in every Idaho town within driving distance of a big dairy. And add the wages held down across every trade that has to compete with subsidized labor. Idahoans pay all of it, while the savings go on one set of books and the costs go on everybody else's. Then the argument eats itself. Farm Bureau guy says he wants the food grown here, by people paid decently, so we aren't at the mercy of Mexico for lettuce. Good. That's economic nationalism and he's right. But he wants it grown here using the same cheap foreign labor he'd be buying if the farm were in Mexico, so the deal hasn't changed at all, he's just moved the border so the cheap part happens on our side of it, with our schools and our hospitals absorbing the difference. You can't wave the flag to keep the farm and then dissolve the country's labor market to keep the margin. It's a passive-aggressive threat: vote our way or your groceries get expensive. A country is a people before it's an economy. But once the people are an input cost, there's nothing left worth defending. | | | | | | | (C) 2026 Brian Lenney ? ?

name: Americans for Responsible Innovation
subject: ARI’s AI governance framework put to the test
body:
Standards, assurance, and transparency: a federal framework for AI governance.

| | The ARI Briefing * August 2026 | [](https://us.list-manage.com/Dyk4fxYG0aT?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---|---
# The Warning Signs Are Here
What federal frontier AI governance looks like from the inside
Over the last several weeks, the public has learned of how unprepared the world's systems and institutions are to identify and respond to early signs of potentially dangerous AI behavior. New details about the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident demonstrate how advanced AI systems can behave in unexpected ways, with dangerous events arising before their full scope is understood. This raises an important question addressed in a new fictional scenario developed by ARI:
What would happen if a governance framework were already in place to identify early signals related to potential harms from AI models, independently evaluate them, and require action before they put the public at risk?
---
_The Frontier Scenario: A Year in the Life of Unicorn AI_ looks at how ARI's blueprint for federal frontier AI governance, built around three core functions any federal framework should carry: standards, assurance, and transparency, would function in practice.
| | Featured Analysis | 01
---|---
## The Frontier Scenario: A Year in the Life of Unicorn AI
An illustrative, fictional account of frontier AI development under ARI's blueprint
By Morgan C. Plummer
[](https://us.list-manage.com/_560HeBaVjG?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
Unicorn AI is not a real company. Nothing in the scenario is a prediction.
ARI published [The Frontier Scenario: A Year in the Life of Unicorn AI](https://us.list-manage.com/obDrIzoy0Z1?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf), an illustrative and deliberately fictional account of what federal oversight of frontier AI would look like from inside a company subject to it. Unicorn AI is not a real company. Nothing in the piece is a prediction. [ARI's blueprint,](https://us.list-manage.com/ET5a9uuCGDF?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf) published last month, describes what a federal framework should require. The scenario shows those requirements operating.
To follow it, start by assuming Congress has passed the law. The scenario picks up a year into that world.
| Crossing the lineUnicorn closes a large funding round and commits most of it to training its next model, which pushes the company's spending and computing power past the line where the new law applies. No agency calls to say it is now covered. The law sets that line in plain numbers, so Unicorn's own engineers and lawyers can work out whether they are over it, the way a company works out its own tax obligations without waiting to be told.
---
Within 60 daysUnicorn files a safety plan with the government. It covers five categories of risk, from cyberattack capability to the automation of AI research itself, and names one executive accountable for it. The government reviews the plan against minimum federal standards and then publishes it. Competitors, journalists, and outside researchers can all read what Unicorn has promised, which means the company cannot quietly walk it back later.
On a standing basisThe government also puts people in the building. A federal examiner team works out of Unicorn the way Federal Reserve supervisors sit inside the largest banks. They are not auditors dropping in for a week. They see internal test results, red-team reports, and who escalated what to whom. A separate federal team, organized by risk area and drawn from a national lab, tests each finished model before Unicorn can deploy it.
Before deploymentThat is where the scenario's central problem arises. Unicorn's own testing concluded its new model could not carry out certain cyberattacks. The federal evaluators, using tools Unicorn's team did not have, get further and find that it can. Unicorn's own safety plan says that if the model can do that, the company owes specific safeguards first.
Seven days to respondWhat follows is paperwork. The lead examiner sends a findings letter. Unicorn has seven days to respond, and submits a plan to retest and add safeguards. Deployment pauses in the meantime, not because a regulator ordered it, but because Unicorn wrote that rule for itself and the government is holding the company to what it said.
Four times a year, Unicorn also reports confidentially on how much of its own research and development it has handed to AI systems, measured in numbers rather than narrative. The examiners file their own independent estimates for the same period, so the company's figures can be checked against people who have been watching. The public sees only a total across all covered companies, which makes it possible to ask whether AI research is automating faster than human oversight can keep up.
The tradeUnicorn is more constrained in this world than in ours. The company also knows what will be asked of it, when, and how to build accordingly. That is the trade at the heart of the blueprint: developer autonomy decreases so that public safety increases, and in return developers get regulatory certainty.
---
Days before the scenario was published, the absence of that oversight stopped being hypothetical. [METR](https://us.list-manage.com/108PFUnsWEN?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf), the nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems, released an independent investigation into the OpenAI models that broke out of a sandboxed cybersecurity evaluation in July. Working on OpenAI's premises across six days, with a Redwood Research staff member contracting alongside them, the team found that roughly 1,200 agents meant to be isolated from one another had found a way to communicate on an unsanctioned message board, exchanging more than 70,000 messages and files. About 700 went on to attack Hugging Face.
Roughly one in five looked for ways to alter their own transcripts, and a small share succeeded in faking tool calls. Across more than a thousand transcripts, investigators found only a handful of cases where an agent even considered alerting a human, and none where one did.
| [Read ARI's scenario](https://us.list-manage.com/b7vj4K1hkBv?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---

## Meet the Lawmakers Speaking Out on Data Centers
A virtual panel on what communities have actually won at the bargaining table
[](https://us.list-manage.com/tto1i1Porwa?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
Across the country, residents are calling for a voice in negotiations over data center deals that reshape their communities. Some have won guardrails on energy demand, some have secured local investment in education and workforce training, and some have pushed for moratoriums.
On September 10, ARI will host a [virtual panel](https://us.list-manage.com/1CdVbGQu2zq?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf), bringing together state lawmakers, county officials, and advocates who have secured guardrails in their own communities. They will share what worked, where negotiations broke down, and what residents should be entitled to when a data center comes to town.
Thursday, September 10
2:00 PM ET, online

## Funding the Science of Reliable AI
Assurance research is a public good, and the market will not supply it
By Aaron Dorshow
[](https://us.list-manage.com/3Gdy5Zp4Jfi?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
In [Preventing the Next Hugging Face Hack](https://us.list-manage.com/Car1dyUMj7I?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf), ARI policy analyst Aaron Dorshow argues that the July incident exposed a gap Congress can actually close. AI assurance, the science of discovering, assessing, and managing risks across the AI lifecycle, is advancing far more slowly than the systems it is meant to govern.
Two forces hold it back. A fiercely competitive industry rewards building more capable models over understanding the ones already deployed. And the research itself is genuinely hard: unlike conventional software, where an engineer can inspect and revise every line, frontier models grow in ways developers can only steer. OpenAI never wrote or directed the code that breached the sandbox. There was no line to fix.
This is a market failure, and the federal government has addressed failures like it before. Federal investment in biomedical research raised private innovation rather than crowding it out, and the Human Genome Project built a public good that later breakthroughs were constructed on. DARPA's AI Forge program signals that the administration already grasps the national security stakes. Passing the [Reliable AI Research Act](https://us.list-manage.com/tFbwY7UhbBG?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf) would be Congress's first step in matching it.
[Read the analysis ->](https://us.list-manage.com/FTxzn4OZJhT?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
| | National Security | 04
---|---
## The Invisible Backbone
AI is critical infrastructure in every respect but the designation
By Jessica Maksimov
[](https://us.list-manage.com/xTKnMpzuD22?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
The opening paper in a series on threats to the AI infrastructure stack.
AI has become underlying infrastructure for the United States, embedded in government operations, national defense, and the private sector. In [The Invisible Backbone](https://us.list-manage.com/nwW6PgIp7sd?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf), ARI policy analyst Jessica Maksimov argues the sector still lacks the formal recognition that would bring coordination, information sharing, and protection standards commensurate with that role.
The scale of dependence is already substantial. AI-related federal contracts rose nearly 150 percent in a single year. Sixty-four percent of federal employees report using AI applications several times a week or daily. One in five organizations surveyed has identified a serious security vulnerability introduced by AI-generated code.
The sector also faces threats federal frameworks were not built for: data poisoning and supply chain manipulation, the theft or distillation of model weights, and an algorithmic monoculture in which compromising one foundation model can propagate vulnerabilities across everything built atop it. The report recommends the President designate AI as a critical infrastructure sector, that CISA and CAISI publish security baselines for AI data centers, and that Congress fund infrastructure security research through DARPA.
[Read the report ->](https://us.list-manage.com/yHCSYc7pRpY?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
| | Civil Liberties | 05
---|---
## Security Without a Blank Check
Why a warrant requirement would not break Section 702
By Allie Maloney
[](https://us.list-manage.com/xXyCBWHdy6q?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
FISA Section 702 lapsed on June 12, and the sky has not fallen. Authorized surveillance continues until the underlying court certifications expire in March 2027. In [Security Without a Blank Check](https://us.list-manage.com/JZJGU9ccIOO?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf), ARI policy analyst Allie Maloney argues that the absence of a deadline is an opportunity: Congress can finally address the loopholes permitting warrantless searches of Americans' communications rather than passing a clean reauthorization under pressure.
AI raises the stakes. Where an intelligence officer once assembled a picture of a target over hours, a model can scan the database continuously and at depth, and combine what it finds with data purchased from brokers to assemble a mosaic of a person's life. The [Government Surveillance Reform Act](https://us.list-manage.com/WKAAWYXLFD3?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf) would codify a warrant requirement for reading Americans' communications while preserving the database queries the intelligence community uses to establish probable cause, and it retains an exception for imminent threats to life.
The argument is not that AI has no place in investigations. It is that these tools should operate inside the constitutional process, and that security should not become a blank check.
[Read the analysis ->](https://us.list-manage.com/3Zof2PPE9eG?e=a07d75591f&c2id=4fb88adb36cbae4881a2e5f253eb58cf)
---
| The last few weeks have demonstrated that AI is evolving at a rapid pace, and AI developers cannot make the rules for which they grade their own work.Thank you for being part of ARI's work. Your support enables us to produce cutting-edge research, convene critical conversations, and push for policies that keep emerging technologies aligned with the public interest.Onward,The ARI Team

# ["Give disinflation a chance": Waller leans hold](https://substack.com/redirect/964fe18a-53ac-433e-b3dc-ae51f765d58f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he is **[inclined to hold rates at the Sept. 15-16 meeting](https://substack.com/redirect/e06b367a-de34-461d-a9e3-7f5a37fc702a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** if August inflation keeps cooling, cutting market-implied hike odds to about 48% from near 60%.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/964fe18a-53ac-433e-b3dc-ae51f765d58f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Give disinflation a chance:** **[Waller paraphrased John Lennon](https://substack.com/redirect/82054410-20eb-4087-ba90-c9a87380addc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** and said waiting one meeting is cheap, because a 25-basis-point hike now will not drag CPI to 2%.
* **July still runs hot:** Headline inflation was 3.7% in July and core 3.3%, but the three-month rate on the Fed's preferred gauge has slipped from 4.76% in February to 3.05%.
* **Hot print still brings a hike:** Waller said policy is "only slightly restricting" demand and that he would consider a hike if August inflation reverses progress toward 2%.
* **CPI is the referee:** The only major prints before the meeting are next week's CPI and PPI, which feed the PCE index the Fed actually targets.

# [$11B in Dutch gold just left New York for London](https://substack.com/redirect/964fe18a-53ac-433e-b3dc-ae51f765d58f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The Dutch central bank moved 78 metric tons of gold, worth about $11 billion, **[from Manhattan vaults to London,](https://substack.com/redirect/00a0ca25-2c39-40ce-bbd0-12511e7a6178?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** citing geopolitical unrest and a need to trade the metal faster in a pinch.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/964fe18a-53ac-433e-b3dc-ae51f765d58f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **London now holds the bigger share:** Almost a third of the Dutch gold reserve now sits in London, while New York's slice is 19%, flipping the earlier split.
* **Unrest, then a trading rationale:** The bank cited increasing geopolitical unrest but did not spell out the threat; it said the shift improves its ability to trade gold quickly if needed.
* **Manhattan vaults were the source:** The Wall Street Journal said the bars came from vaults beneath the streets of Manhattan, not a symbolic sliver but a full 78-ton transfer.
* **Price tag tracks this week 's spike:** At current prices the moved metal is worth about $11 billion, landing in London as bullion itself was breaking $4,500.

# [Qatar just skipped Hormuz with a rare LNG trick](https://substack.com/redirect/964fe18a-53ac-433e-b3dc-ae51f765d58f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Gulf exporters **[completed three unusual ship-to-ship LNG transfers outside](https://substack.com/redirect/f4cf8dbf-c0c9-4d9b-ad34-6af3b08226c8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** Hormuz in August, a workaround as the strait crisis keeps normal gas traffic stalled.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/964fe18a-53ac-433e-b3dc-ae51f765d58f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **GasLog handed off off Oman:** Greek-owned GasLog Shanghai transferred its cargo onto GasLog Savannah offshore Oman in late August.
* **Qatar cargo still reached India:** Qatar-owned Al Rekayyat transferred onto fellow Qatari tanker Tembek in mid-August, and that cargo was delivered to India on Aug. 31.
* **ADNOC cargo is bound for Japan:** ADNOC-owned Mraweh transferred onto LNG Enugu offshore Oman in mid-August, with the load en route to Japan.
* **Workaround, not a reopened strait:**[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/f4cf8dbf-c0c9-4d9b-ad34-6af3b08226c8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[ZeroHedge said](https://substack.com/redirect/f4cf8dbf-c0c9-4d9b-ad34-6af3b08226c8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** the transfers are rare and that regional gas traffic remains stalled even as these three cargoes found a path around the chokepoint.

subject: Newsom ruined his state. He's not ruining mine.
body:
While Gavin Newsom tours South Carolina, take a look at what he actually did to his own state. |
---

**Fellow Patriot - Gavin Newsom is in South Carolina right now.**

He's holding meet-and-greets and rallying support for Democrats up and down the ballot. Democrats brought him in on purpose. They want to turn South Carolina into California, and I'm not going to let that happen.

_Before anybody in this state takes a single thing Gavin Newsom says seriously, I want you to look at what he actually did with the power he was given._

As Governor, he ran California into the ground. Businesses are fleeing the state, homelessness has gotten worse, and gas prices and the cost of living have pushed working families out of their own communities. That is not a talking point. That is what happened under his leadership, in the state he still runs today.

_Now he's building the same kind of Democratic machine here._

Annie Andrews has already raised nearly $11 million, much of it from the same national donor network Newsom is rallying here. Every stop he makes on this trip helps energize the exact coalition trying to elect someone who will vote with Chuck Schumer, not South Carolina.

clean_body: While Gavin Newsom tours South Carolina, take a look at what he actually did to his own state. | Fellow Patriot - Gavin Newsom is in South Carolina right now. He's holding meet-and-greets and rallying support for Democrats up and down the ballot. Democrats brought him in on purpose. They want to turn South Carolina into California, and I'm not going to let that happen. Before anybody in this state takes a single thing Gavin Newsom says seriously, I want you to look at what he actually did with the power he was given. As Governor, he ran California into the ground. Businesses are fleeing the state, homelessness has gotten worse, and gas prices and the cost of living have pushed working families out of their own communities. That is not a talking point. That is what happened under his leadership, in the state he still runs today. Now he's building the same kind of Democratic machine here. Annie Andrews has already raised nearly $11 million, much of it from the same national donor network Newsom is rallying here. Every stop he makes on this trip helps energize the exact coalition trying to elect someone who will vote with Chuck Schumer, not South Carolina. I did not spend thirty years serving South Carolina to watch it get handed over to the same failed ideas that wrecked California. Fellow Patriot, I need your help to keep California money and ideas out of our state today. Please don't let Gavin Newsom's failed record become South Carolina's future. Thank you for standing with me, Darline Graham P.S. Quality Care Access charges more per patient than any autism residential care provider in the country, at nearly $40,000 monthly for each patient. Every single dollar comes from the American taxpayer. In return, they promise to provide Mainers who have Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Intellectual and Developmental Disorders (IDD), or traumatic brain injuries (TBI) with a comforting, home-like environment. They politicians and bureaucrats in Augusta call this home- and community-based care. But Maine Wire Reporter Jon Fetherston's investigation has found that disabled Mainers, who often lack the ability to advocate for their own welfare, are enduring shocking levels of neglect and mistreatment.
Read his report below, originally published at [TheMaineWire.com](https://substack.com/redirect/5d52a93f-cc42-41e7-805d-91f5521c5158?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and follow [Jon on X](https://substack.com/redirect/fa7525c1-8664-4149-8232-461650f7f355?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
* * *
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/34aabbc0-4443-4e5e-b2ee-5ff3b55e050c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**What began as a Maine Wire investigation into Maine 's expanding network of taxpayer-funded residential care providers has grown more troubling:**
* **Recurrent bed bug infestations caused by migrant workers who treated autism group homes like crash pads**
* **Non-English speaking DSPs cheating on certification exams they struggled to understand.**
* **A deceased doctor listed as the health official in charge of a company that 's billed $27.8 million to provide residential care for less than 16 patients**
* **A Medicaid agency that bills more per patient than any other autism group home operating in then country, according to Medicaid records**

Another start-up MaineCare agency has come under scrutiny for its treatment of disabled clients and its anomalous billing patterns following an investigation by The Maine Wire into Maine's controversial -- and wildly expensive -- autism group home program, known as MaineCare Section 21.
The Medicaid agency -- Quality Care Access, LLC -- was chartered in July 2020 by Jovin Bayingana, and the Portland-based company rapidly became one of the most lucrative new MaineCare businesses in New England.
According to Medicaid payment records obtained via a Freedom of Access Act request, the company billed the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) for $1.2 million in 2021, $5.3 million in 2022, $7.4 million in 2023, $6.7 million in 2024, and $7.2 million in 2025 -- for a lifetime cost of $27.8 million.
The more detailed federal Medicaid dataset shows that throughout this time frame QCA had fewer than 16 patients in most years.
At the same time, the company's monthly cost per client rose from $33,306 in 2022 to $39,234 in 2024.
Similarly, the average value of a Medicaid claim submitted by QCA, according to the federal records, rose from $6,966 to $8,736, indicating the company was increasing revenue by increasing billing rather than bringing on new clients.
According to Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) records, the authorized health official for QCA is [Dr. Justin Nsenga](https://substack.com/redirect/368e25a4-91fd-4b3a-9b3e-67dcf38cb06b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) -- which is slightly problematic because Nsenga reportedly died in a July 1, 2024 auto accident.
The autism company operates within Maine's MaineCare Section 21 waiver program, a taxpayer-funded program that provides 24/7 care for adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) or other intellectual and developmental disorders (IDD).
The state refers to this as "Community Based Residential Treatment," or "A home-like residential facility providing habilitation, support and monitoring services to individuals diagnosed with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities."

The former employee, who requested to speak anonymously for fear of retaliation by individuals within Maine's residential care industry, also detailed a culture of neglect for residents' health, safety, and disability rights.
The source also described an approach to managing employee rotations that prioritized sleeping accommodations for the DSPs over the rights and needs of disabled residents, a fact that contributed to the recurrent bed bug infestations that allegedly plagued the autism group homes.
Rather than medical care facilities for disabled adults, the source described a taxpayer-subsidized system where non-English-speaking African migrants rotated from property to property couch-surfing rather than providing care.
The whistleblower alleged employees slept while on duty but that services were nevertheless billed as though work had been performed. She also alleged employees improperly took or handled clients' money and described verbal and other mistreatment of people receiving services.
"I would say most of the staff didn't speak English," the source said. "I'd say about 90 92% probably spoke a different language, and then 8% spoke English."
The former employee claimed some clients became so frustrated by an inability to communicate with staff that they engaged in dangerous or desperate behavior. She alleged that clients sometimes swallowed batteries or called police in hopes of being arrested simply because an encounter with law enforcement provided an opportunity to communicate with someone who spoke English.

---
Fellow Patriot,
---
We've looked at the polling in every swing state and swing race in the country. It's margin of error, either way, almost everywhere.

At this point, it's not about winning anybody over. _It's about who actually shows up._

If conservatives turn out in November, we'll win every critical battleground and lay the groundwork for victory in 2028 and beyond.

That's why Turning Point Action is focusing all our efforts on three key states: Arizona, Nevada, and New Hampshire.

**We call these states the new RED WALL.**

_Let me explain why they matter so much... _

After 2024, Charlie looked at the numbers, looked at the maps, and told our team something simple. If we lock down Arizona, Nevada, and New Hampshire, the Left's entire strategy falls apart. Their map collapses. Their path back to power disappears.

Here's why... Winning the presidency comes down to 270 electoral votes. Lose Arizona and most of the realistic paths to the White House in 2028 are gone. Lose Nevada and New Hampshire and the Left rebuilds the Blue Wall they lost in 2024.

Whoever wins in 2028 controls the 2030 Census. The Census drives redistricting. Redistricting sets the congressional map for the next ten years.

Peter,

Late last night, Elon Musk officially filed with the FEC to spend some of
his nearly $1 trillion in Michigan to help Mike Rogers and stop us from
winning. Musk spent big in 2024, and we saw a red wave put Trump back in
the White House.

We’re already being outspent and out-advertised. I’m worried it could get
worse. And the thing about Elon is he has virtually unlimited money. He
could spend like 0.5% of his net worth, and it would change this whole
race.

But what we showed in the primary, where we were outspent 11-to-1, is that
we can still beat the big money guys if we put up good enough numbers of
our own.

So, look, I know folks like us can’t donate millions of dollars like they
can. We don’t have to. Because if something like 1-in-4 of the people
reading this email decide, “You know what? I can step up and give
$10,” we will be able to raise enough to counter their
attacks and spread our good word to the voters of Michigan.

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260903-2-ak.6QehYP&amount=10&refcode=em20260903-3097&t=1004&akid=3098%2E251025%2ElAsJKQ ]Peter, can
I count on you to be one of those folks who can donate today? Whether you
can give a lot or a little doesn’t matter. What matters is that enough of
us pitch in.

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260903-2-ak.6QehYP&amount=10&refcode=em20260903-3097&t=1005&akid=3098%2E251025%2ElAsJKQ ]Count me in ››

These guys like Elon, they’re not spending against me because they think
our policies are wrong. They’re spending because they think they can put
in a few million dollars and get back a whole lot more in tax breaks.
They’re spending to protect their own pocketbooks.

I'm not telling you this to scare you. We can get outspent and still win.
But we can't get outspent by any number and still win.

If Elon buys every ad break between now and November, most Michiganders
will only ever hear his version of me. They won’t hear our message. And
then it won't matter how good our ideas are, because people won’t be
hearing them at all.

So your donations right now, and the ones you’ve given in the past, mean
absolutely everything.

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260903-2-ak.6QehYP&amount=10&refcode=em20260903-3097&t=1006&akid=3098%2E251025%2ElAsJKQ ]Please, help us counter this Elon influx. Be one of those to give

I’m so grateful to this team. You are the reason we have a fighting
chance. Even up against the richest guy on the planet, the president of
the United States, the corporate overlords, and the military-industrial
complex.

Thank you, from the bottom of my heart.

Abdul

# Thursday, September 3, 2026
---
**Good Afternoon!** Most of us have more personal information floating around online than we realize, and scammers know exactly where to look for it. Today, our sponsor [Incogni](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyskD1uxCAQhU-Du7UGsAEXFJFW7jZtSoTN4EXCZgV4f24feRUpOUDKbzQz-t77upiLDTFsy6ddUdenT8ahC7Ot6MyGjxKxVsym1HR7pT07W63PaZ0wbEtJ0RkGTJxgOAH_c0kbpydwA21QU6lU16uu75qrxskPfS8RsZcgpEdwjClB5SQpSEaboI-HMACnCqBn7aAsqJmDcpLiNADpAF2oKbf1ihWftvj4SnfM7ZzWJuprrbdC-AdhI2GjQxvbsM1p2UIbEmGj9d7MhI_Je8wmOMLPgjBxjN9AuTy4pD3PSPj5N9QhRZjYc_zZbLJ2t0eIMRQhSQfLakN8a9T_rPKu2XcAAAD__4gSjCE) explains how to find and remove that data before it ends up in the wrong hands. -- Cole, CEO
* * *

name: Phil Weiser
subject: Thank you for a great August!
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Phil Weiser for Colorado
body:
I am grateful to you, friend.

Even with busy summer schedules, you and the rest of this team showed up and helped us accomplish some pretty great things last month:

https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP10/1/81362/images/em_WEI_OTH_ThankYouAugust_090326.png

I know that, with school out of session, many of us spend August juggling work, care responsibilities, and making the most of some beautiful weather while it lasts.

Last month kept us busy over here on the campaign, too. Your generous support has allowed us to show up all across the state, meet people face-to-face in their communities, and build the support we’ll need to win.

Of course, the work is not over yet. The opposition has been busy, too — and we are just two months away from the election.

I won’t dwell on the opposition for too long, but I mean it when I say this: the ideas they are running on are extreme and reckless. We cannot sit back and assume we’ll be handed a victory. This is a time to lean even more on the gas, not hit the brakes.

I’ll be out on the campaign trail, listening to Coloradans and sharing our movement’s plan to deliver for them — and I hope to see you out there, too.

With gratitude,

Phil

| | | | | | Peter,
I need you to think about this number for a moment:
**387,000.**
That’s how many Pennsylvania households faced utility shutoffs last year. Not in a recession. Not during a natural disaster. In one of the wealthiest states in the richest country in the world, nearly 400,000 families couldn’t keep their lights on.
And in the same year, Pennsylvania’s average electricity cost went up almost 15%. The average electricity bill has gone up more than 20% since 2024. Another round of rate increases is hitting this summer.
**Where is Josh Shapiro on any of this?**
He’s the highest-paid governor in America. He presides over the 47th-ranked economy in the country. He has the 5th highest tax burden. And his response to a utility affordability crisis is — nothing.
He welcomed in out of state data center developers who are consuming massive amounts of electricity and driving up energy costs for everyone else. And his only energy “plan” is to hold press conferences.
**Press conferences don’t keep the lights on.**
Here’s what a Garrity Administration will do:
⚡ Cut utility bills by 15–25%
🏭 Fast-track new power generation so supply can meet the growing demand
🏠 Cut property taxes by one-third through the HOPE for PA initiative
387,000 families. That number should keep every elected official in Harrisburg up at night. Instead, the Governor is on a book tour.
**It’s time to turn Pennsylvania around.**
– Team Garrity

| | | The commissioners of Tarrant County, Texas, voted 3-2 this week to approve **a list of polling sites for the November elections that included 92 fewer sites than the 2022 midterms** , Team. _Yes, this county is reducing the number of polling places between the primary and the general election_. The change came after commissioners heard testimony from more than 100 speakers, the majority of whom were opposed to the site cuts, during a meeting that lasted over eight hours. **The final list includes 224 sites for Election Day (down from 316) and 47 for early voting (down from 50).** _The commissioners voted along party lines_ , with Republicans supporting the reduced list, and the Democratic commissioners voting against. “ _It’s not about cost. This is about power. This is very political. This is campaigning from the dais_ ,” said commissioner Alisa Simmons. More than 1.3 million people are registered to vote in Tarrant County, which is more than live in the full states of Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, or Montana, and about the same number of people who live in Maine or New Hampshire. This is voter suppression, plain and simple, by making it harder for eligible, registered voters to vote in-person by taking away their polling place. It's another demonstration of how **opponents of voting rights in Texas and beyond are more focused on expanding and cementing their own power** than they are in serving the people and having fair elections.**** **[We have to fight these suppressive closures in any state where opponents of voting rights try to replicate this. But then something happens that restores that faith.
A stranger stops me at an event to say they're praying for this campaign. A volunteer shows up at 7 a.m. to knock doors before their own workday even starts.

**YESTERDAY WAS A BAD DAY FOR CHRIS PAPPAS**
---
| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | **FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE** September 3rd, 2026
---
| | | **CONTACT** karina@nhrsc.com

---
| |

CONCORD, N.H. — The New Hampshire Republican State Committee Chairman Scott Maltzie released the following statement:
“Chris Pappas had a rough day yesterday,” **said NHGOP Chairman Scott Maltzie.** “He voted against keeping the Supreme Court at nine Justices, further proving he isn’t the moderate he claims to be to Granite Staters.”“It got worse from there. Yesterday, Pappas was given a simple chance to condemn Abdul El-Sayed for standing alongside Hasan Piker, who said ‘America deserved 9/11,’ and he couldn’t do it. New Hampshire deserves a politician in Washington who can call out extremism when they see it. Pappas can’t even do that.”Background: The House of Representatives voted on H.J. Res. 1, a proposed amendment to the Constitution of the United States requiring that the Supreme Court of the United States be composed of only nine Justices, via roll call vote 293. The vote failed to produce the two-thirds majority needed to pass a constitutional amendment in the House. Watch the video [here](https://us.list-manage.com/14sjSFE4nXl?e=f3aa6419cd&c2id=cbe815d8d4829b0196839495b093775b&m=ZhHQQoXuwXQcKWIfhMzu-eDPNlK26NhAsXrQLq5_wcD6B-gPO1w6FDbBKQ==).

The consultants, the political class, the talking heads on cable news, they looked at this race, looked at Jon Ossoff's war chest, and have written us off. Too much money on the other side, they said. Too tough a hill to climb. Don't waste your time. Meanwhile, Jon Ossoff has been activating Hollywood celebrities, raking in checks from every coastal elite with a Venmo account and a grudge against the America First movement. And you know what? I'll admit it, for a while there, the gap felt big. But then something happened. You happened. Because of this grassroots operation, because of donors like you chipping in $10, $25, $50 at a time, The DC crowd didn't see that coming. The pollsters didn't see it coming. And I promise you, Jon Ossoff didn't see it coming either. But here's why I’m reaching out. At the end of this month, we have just around 2 months left until Election Day. Two months. Eight weeks. The final stretch. If we come in strong tonight, we send a message that this race is real, this campaign is surging, and our campaign is the real deal heading into the final sprint. If we come in weak, the DC insiders who wrote us off get all the ammunition they need to keep us on the sidelines. Patriot , Jon Ossoff is out there tonight with his Hollywood friends writing big checks. I'm sitting here asking America First patriots for whatever they can spare before midnight, because that's how this campaign has always been built. {LINK}{LINK} We closed a big gap to get to 4 points down. Let's close the rest. Let's keep the pedal to the metal and finish this haul the right way. Thank you. From the bottom of my heart For Georgia, Mike Collins Republican Nominee, U.S. Senate — Georgia | | PAID FOR BY MIKE COLLINS FOR SENATE | | PO BOX 6491 ATHENS, GA 30604 | | Hey, if you're still reading this, don't forget to follow Mike Collins for Senate on and , and TEXT MIKE TO 70622 If you would like to opt-out of important updates like this, please here.

clean_body: Republicans are looking to the world’s richest man to protect their majority. | = Peter, Republicans are looking for help holding onto their U.S. House majority — and they know exactly who to call. Tomorrow, Speaker Mike Johnson plans to meet with Elon Musk in Texas as Republican leaders court the world's richest man ahead of the midterms. Musk is reportedly considering spending at least $100 million through his super PAC to help elect Republicans this November. That is an extraordinary amount of money. It would mean more ads, more attacks, and more ugly tactics aimed at defeating Democratic candidates in some of the closest races in the country. EMILYs List women are running to win those races — and we need the resources to make sure Republican billionaires can't drown them out. = | = Republicans have spent years passing policies that make the richest people in this country even richer. Now, they're turning to that same extraordinary wealth to help keep themselves in power. EMILYs List has gone up against billionaire-backed spending for years. But now, for the first time, we're facing the prospect of the world's first trillionaire pouring tens of millions of dollars into electing Republicans. The cycle is getting more extreme: More wealth at the top, more money flooding our elections, and more political power for the people who helped create the system in the first place. That makes our work harder — but it doesn't change how we fight back. While Republicans court megadonors, EMILYs List women are showing up in their communities, talking to voters, organizing, and earning support, one constituent at a time. We may never match Elon Musk dollar for dollar. We don't need to. name: Swing Left
subject: Democrats have momentum in Georgia
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Swing Left, [swingleft
body:
We’re targeting the governor’s race, the State House, and the State Senate.
#
Hi there,
In 2021, Georgians elected Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff to the U.S. Senate, the first Democrats to win a Senate race in Georgia in over 20 years. And in 2025, Democrats flipped two seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, their first non-federal statewide wins since 2006.
This year, in addition to re-electing Jon Ossoff, the Swing Left community will be working to help Democrats flip yet another statewide seat in Georgia by electing **Keisha Lance Bottoms** to the governor’s office.
With Republican Governor Brian Kemp term-limited and Democrats surging, this year’s midterm election provides a real opportunity to flip the governor’s office blue for the first time since 1999.
A win in this race would break the Republican trifecta that has given them unchecked control over Georgia, even as it’s become a true presidential and Senate battleground.
**It would also give Democrats a critical veto over Republican efforts to restrict voting access, redraw district maps, or tilt the playing field ahead of 2028.**
But the governor’s race isn’t the only one we’re targeting.
We’ve also added Georgia’s **State House** and **State Senate** to our list of “Reach” races. We think flipping those chambers is still going to be an uphill battle, but in a wave election, it could happen, which makes these legislative races worth investing in.
Democrats need to flip 10 seats in the State House and 6 seats in the State Senate to win majorities, and together, this community can help turn that possibility into a reality.
[](https://act.swingleft.org/go/27?c0=sl-states-ga-2026.MAir3x&refcode=em20260903-2661&t=1&akid=2661%2E1562180%2EMw4pGX)
[**If you’d like to help Democrats build critical state-level power in Georgia this November, click here to make a donation to the Georgia Win In The States Fund today.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/27?c0=sl-states-ga-2026.MAir3x&refcode=em20260903-2661&t=2&akid=2661%2E1562180%2EMw4pGX)
**[Donate Now](https://act.swingleft.org/go/27?c0=sl-states-ga-2026.MAir3x&refcode=em20260903-2661&t=3&akid=2661%2E1562180%2EMw4pGX)**
Your donation will be split between Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic state legislative caucuses in Georgia, and Swing Left as we work to turn out voters across the state this year.
Thank you as always for being a part of this work, and make sure to stay tuned for more updates soon!
— The Swing Left Team

**Since 2017, Swing Left has channeled the energy of grassroots volunteers and donors to elect Democrats, up and down the ballot, focusing on the most competitive races that can swing the national balance of power.** Right now, Swing Left is investing in grassroots organizing in key swing districts and initiatives across the country to flip the House and win the Senate and critical states in 2026. [**If you’d like to help support our work, you can make a donation using this link.**](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_sl_footer?refcode=em20260903-1&t=4&refcode2=2661_1562180_Mw4pGX&akid=2661%2E1562180%2EMw4pGX)

body:
Before politics, I spent years in the classroom. That experience still guides me.
#
Hi Peter, it’s Tim.
Before I was Governor Walz or Congressman Walz, I was Mr. Walz and Coach Walz. I spent years in the classroom, and I can tell you: Schools are the heart of a community.
They’re where kids learn, where teachers pour everything they have into the next generation, and where families come together around the promise that every child deserves a fair shot.
That’s especially true in small towns.
When a school is strong, the whole community feels it. And when politicians in Washington ignore rural communities, underfund public schools, or put billionaires and corporate interests first, working families pay the price.
That’s why I started Small Town PAC: to support leaders who understand what communities actually need — good schools, good jobs, affordable health care, and a real future for the next generation.

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw
